subtopic: SALE OP CANADIAN MEAT AND MEAT PRODUCTS IN JAPAN
SALE OP CANADIAN MEAT AND MEAT PRODUCTS IN JAPAN
speechtext: What action is the Canadian Government taking to explore the Japanese market with a view to the sale of Canadian meat and meat products following the agreement between Australia and Japan for the sale of Australian beef?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: SALE OP CANADIAN MEAT AND MEAT PRODUCTS IN JAPAN
speechtext:
There is no agreement between the Governments of Australia and Japan for the sale of Australian beef. Indeed, the Japanese Government imposes quantitative import restrictions on beef imported from Australia as it does from any other country. The fact that the greater part of the Japanese quota for the past fiscal year was filled by Australia was due largely to the price advantage enjoyed by the lower-priced Australian product. So far as Canada is concerned, official representations have been made on a number of occasions, requesting the Japanese authorities to liberalize the importation of this and other Canadian products still subject to quantitative import restrictions when entering Japan, On the promotional side the Canadian Government has been actively exploring the Japanese market for meat and meat products by means of: 1. Sponsorship of a solo food show in Japan in 1969 where Canadian food processors displayed Canadian meat and meat products-. 2. Sponsorship of a beef cutting demonstration in Japan late in 1968 where the high quality of Canadian beef was

stressed. 3. Sponsorship of a meat mission in 1969 from Japan where the high quality of Canadian meats was demonstrated to Japanese processors, wholesalers, importers and Government officials. 4. A planned Canadian meat quality demonstration in Japan in October 1970 to emphasize the high quality of Canadian meat and meat products. 5. A planned solo food show in Japan late this year or early next year at which Canadian meat products are expected to be prominently featured.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: SUMMER EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
1. It is estimated that of the students who will be attending universities and colleges in the fall, 385,000 will be seeking temporary employment this summer.
2.	This figure represents an increase of 35,000 over the summer of 1969.
3.	It is expected that of the students who will be entering secondary institutions in grade 10 and above in the fall, 255,000 will be seeking employment this summer, an increase of 23,000 over the summer of 1969.
4.	It is estimated that 25,000 students at the post-secondary level were unable to locate employment in the summer of 1969. Information is not available on the number of secondary school students who were unable to locate employment in the summer of 1969.
5.	The Department of Manpower and Immigration is engaged in an intensive program to assist students to find summer employment. This program includes a national and local advertising campaign to encourage the hiring of students. Public awareness and involvement is being encouraged by promotion of and participation in student summer employment committees at the national, regional and local levels for which a sum of $260,000.00 has been allocated. Canada Manpower Centres across Canada are providing an employment service to students as well as consultative assistance to those students developing self-help or entrepreneurial activities. For this purpose,

376 student counsellors are being hired to assist permanent Canada Manpower Centre staff. speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: PROGRAM TO LOCATE EMPLOYMENT FOR OLDER WORKERS
speechtext:

I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Last week I drew to the attention of the government the fact that

May 13, 1970
Inquiries of the Ministry the Canadian Merchant Service Guild was accusing the Department of Transport of strikebreaking because it was issuing special permits to unqualified persons to operate the Haida Transporter. subtopic: WEST COAST TOWBOAT STRIKE-ALLEGED STRIKEBREAKING ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
This is a very complex question, Mr. Speaker. I will do my best to answer it within the time I am allowed.
Under normal circumstances there is provision in the regulations for the issuing of certificates to certain, in the strict sense of the word, unqualified persons. In the case of the west coast, the number of these in any one year rarely exceeds seven or eight. This particular case falls well within the normal requirements and consequently we have issued the permits on that basis. I wish to say, however, that if there were to be any demonstrable or unusual increase in the number of requests, bearing in mind there are rarely more than seven or eight in one year we would look very closely and carefully before moving in that direction.

subtopic: WEST COAST TOWBOAT STRIKE-ALLEGED STRIKEBREAKING ACTIVITIES
speechtext: I ask the minister to look into the fact that the crew of the Haida Transporter are covered by the collective bargaining which is now in dispute and that the Canadian Merchant Service Guild considers that the issuing of these special permits to enable the ship to sail constitutes strikebreaking. subtopic: WEST COAST TOWBOAT STRIKE-ALLEGED STRIKEBREAKING ACTIVITIES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have taken it into consideration. It is a very difficult matter to decide. The primary responsibility of the Department of Transport is for safety and ship manning. The issue here is whether or not we should change established regulations because of a labour dispute in that particular area. I have emphasized that should this become an inordinately large practice or effort by the ship owners, we would certainly look at it much more closely. I must emphasize that to my knowledge the present instance is the only one where permits have been issued, and the norm against which we would judge this is the total of seven or eight permits we normally grant in any one year. In short, I do not anticipate any mass applications of this kind.

A few weeks ago, Mr. Speaker, I had the great pleasure of introducing in the House a bill on the prevention of pollution in Arctic waters which clearly sets forth under what conditions those waters will be open to shipping, without endangering the quality of the water or the ecological balance in the Canadian North. Today, I am equally pleased to move second reading of a bill entitled "An Act to amend the Yukon Act, the Northwest Territories Act and the Territorial Lands Act".
The aim of this bill is twofold. On the one hand, it is aimed at promoting the constitutional development of both territories, in the sense that it will enable their residents to assume more responsibility in the day-to-day administration of their respective governments. On the other hand, it will enable the federal government to better protect the environment. Essentially, the North has been left in its primitive stage and we must take immediate steps so that the development of its resources will continue without jeopardizing the delicate ecological balance of those regions.
The government of Canada has very special responsibilities towards the northern territories. Although the area covers a vast surface, which represents almost 40 per cent of the total surface of Canada, it has less than 1 per cent of the Canadian population. A great number of the inhabitants are Indians or Eskimos still attached to their traditional way of life. Being far from great population and production centres, those two territories are still largely unexplored. The transportation problems and the weather conditions are obviously quite difficult. For all those reasons, the North must still rely on the assistance of the federal government to develop its resources, protect its ecosystem and play a more important role in the national life. The territories are dependent on the central government for the legislation establishing the 
structure of their own government and I suggest that the legislation be again amended, in order to meet their present needs and to maintain an harmonious balance among the requirements of political, economic and social progress in those areas.
There is a close relation between the welfare of the inhabitants of the North and the development of northern resources. This relation has become more than ever significant, as the Yukon and the Mackenzie district-which is part of the Northwest Territories-have become major centres of investment and have acquired an international importance, as reservoirs of raw materials. Very important mines are in operation at Pine Point in the Northwest Territories as well as at Faro and Clinton Creek, in the Yukon. The northern mining industry has reached an exceptional development level in the last few years: let us merely mention that mining production in the Canadian North which was less than $30 million in 1964, will exceed $200 million this year. But the most spectacular strides are still to come.
Northern Canada's oil and gas potential has generated unprecedented activity in the Mackenzie delta and the Arctic islands. This activity will most certainly bring new material benefits to the population but at the same time will not fail to complicate its way of life. The people of the North expect, and rightly so, that improvement in their living standard will be accompanied by the right to play a more active part in their government. These proposed amendments to the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories Act have been drafted to this end. The amendment to the Territorial Lands Act, that I am also asking the House to consider, is intended to protect the surface of such lands.

The introduction of this bill follows closely behind two important pieces of legislation that I submitted to the House and whose object was to protect northern wafers: an Act respecting inland water resources in the Yukon Territory and Northwest Territories, introduced in March, and the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, introduced in April.
It may be useful to remind the House of the evolution of government in the Canadian North. All the citizens elect representatives to the territorial councils, which have legislative powers similar to those held by the provincial Legislatures, except in the field of national resources. Judicially, the Commissioner of

each territory remains responsible to the federal government; in practice, however, he is a resident of the territories, he examines the wishes of the Council and he takes into account the interests of the local population.
In the Yukon, there is since 1908 a Council entirely elected by the people. Now it has seven members. Until 1951, the four members of the Council of the Northwest Territories were appointed. After 1951, three elected representatives for the district of Mackenzie were added to the Council. In 1954, with the addition of a fourth elected representative, the Council consisted of nine members. At that time the eastern Arctic, that is the Keewatin district and Baffin Island, had no representative. In 1966, however, the number of members on the Council was increased to twelve, of whom three were elected by the eastern Arctic representatives. Today seven of the council's twelve members are elected and five are appointed.
In the Yukon, the participation of councillors, at the executive level, started in 1960, when was established the Advisory Committee on Finance, made up of three members of the Council, whose task is to look into the estimates before they are submitted to the Council. The experience gained by that committee, as well as the existence since 1898 of a permanent territorial public service have made it possible for the Yukon to take one more step towards autonomy. Closer links should now be established between the executive and legislative functions of the Yukon government.
The Northwest Territories have not had the same long administrative experience at the local level. Hon. members will remember Mr. Speaker, that a few years ago it was considered that the Northwest Territories would be better handled if they were divided into two sections and two bills for this purpose were brought forward in the House. There were at the time many people who believed that separate political units should be established in view of the social and economic differences between the inhabitants of the western Arctic and those of the eastern territories. It is a fact that the valley of the Mackenzie river was enjoying an economic boom and also had a greater population, whereas the District of Keewatin, the Arctic islands and Baffin Island were still very undeveloped. Almost the whole population of the districts of Keewatin and Franklin were Eskimos who were not, at the time, directly represented at the Territorial Council.

Therefore, it was decided in 1965 to create an advisory commission on the development of the Northwest Territories government, that is the Carrothers Commission. Its members travelled through the territories, consulted the inhabitants and reported to the federal government in the fall of 1966.
As expected, the Advisory Commission realized that the people's most ardent desire was to have a Territorial government that would administer local affairs right on the spot. The Commission recommended Yellowknife as the capital of the Northwest Territories, and the Commissioner and his administrative staff therefore left Ottawa to settle there in September 1967. The gradual transfer of the government services of the Department of Northern Development to the new seat of government at Yellowknife was effected according to a well defined plan. Such a transfer of administrative duties from one level of government to another and from a well organized centre to a completely new framework, has been obviously a tremendous job. When I addressed the Yukon and Northwest Territories councils in November last in connection with the development of their territorial governments, I told them that our two main objectives were to protect and promote the legitimate interests of those living in the North, especially Indians and Eskimos, and to comply with the wishes of the population by making it more self-governing. I then pointed out that our review of the development of government in the North, as a result of the recommendations of the Carrothers Commission and of the various proposals made in this connection by both territorial councils, led us to the main conclusion that the present borders of the territories should not be changed. The delicacy of ecological relationships is much greater in the north than it is in southern Canada. Those relationships are different there because of climatic conditions, geography, topography and the like. In southern Canada, because of the more temperate climate, nature can heal its wounds more readily and tolerate destructive influences more readily than in the north. In the north, because of the climate and the delicate ecological balance it is not always possible for nature to repair damage done to her.

Since the federal government recognizes bilingualism, I am surprised to see that this bill contains no provision to guarantee one way or another the right to bilingualism. Some may say that there are very few French-speaking people in those areas, but a few years from now there may be a sufficient number to prompt the government to establish right now a bilingual system. And even if there were only a few French-speaking residents, I believe that under the definition itself of Canada and of federalism-people boast so much about it in Quebec at the present time-any law reform or any establishment of new systems should be coupled with the creation of genuine bilingualism.

I had the honour to serve for 2J years as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and National Resources, now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing). I believe that this bill reflects a growing movement toward responsible government in the territories.
I think that the impetus given to resource development, to education, health and housing and to the bringing of our native peoples into the mainstream of Canadian life within these territories-all of this achieved by the present and the previous government within the last seven years-is to the credit of the Canadian people. I am not saying that the process is by any means completed. I am not saying that the situation is entirely satisfactory. I think that the interest this Parliament has given to the issue of sovereignty in the north, to the issue of effective control over our northern territories and over our northern seas, the interest and the commitment of the Canadian people, represented in this Parliament in the legislation which the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development recently introduced, and the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of this country in the short term he has been Prime Minister has already visited the north on three separate occasions, indicate a particular interest, a particular commitment of this government, on behalf of the Canadian people, toward those territories which, as my colleague said earlier, represent over 1,300,000 square miles, some 40 per cent of the Canadian land mass but more particularly toward those 40,000 people who live as Canadians north of 60.
I believe that this Parliament and the people of Canada consider our north to be a distinctive asset, something that distinguishes us from the United States, something that gives us a perspective entirely different from that of the United States, a perspective which is rather unique. Mr. Speaker, I have looked at a number of the recommendations of the Carrothers Commission report. It is absolutely incorrect for the Minister of Justice-although he did restrict himself to questions dealing with the administration of justice in the territories-or the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to suggest that there has been any substantial compliance with the major recommendations of this report.
Where, Mr. Speaker, is the executive council? In this bill there is provision for the appointment of certain people to act, but there is no legislative acceptance of the principle of an executive council with specific duties, with specific individuals charged with the administration of certain areas of government responsibility. The Carrothers Commission strongly suggested that in this halfway-house between territorial status and provincial status the name of the legislative body should be changed to "legislative assembly." This has been requested, and what harm would it have done? Why should not the Council of the Northwest Territories be the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories, and the Council of the Yukon be the Legislative Assembly of the Yukon?
What about the question of economic development? This is a very sad, difficult and serious problem. In a press release dated March 31, 1970, the minister stated with some pride:
The territorial administration will have grown from less than 100 persons when it moved to Yellowknife in 1967 to about 1,700 after the eastern Arctic transfer.
I say "shades of Parkinson" when I read that, Mr. Speaker. In any event, of the nonIndian and non-Eskimo people in the Northwest Territories 1,700 plus their wives and dependents are government people and a very substantial number are employed by large
Yukon and Territorial Lands Acts corporations and companies in the territories. As I see it, there is not much opportunity for individuals from the southern part of Canada to carve out a career and a future in the Northwest Territories. I think the situation has probably grown worse rather than better since 1966 when the Carrothers Commission stated at page 172 of volume I:
It is a cold statistic that the average income of the Indian and Eskimo is one-sixth that of the national average, that the infant mortality rate is more than four times the national average, that the life expectancy of those who survive infancy is decades shorter than that of the white man, that the per cent of the uneducated element in the labour force, mainly Indians and Eskimos, is 24 times higher than the national average. These statements are a translation into impersonal statistics of packingcase houses, of tents and igloos, of primitive sanitation and bad water, of pernicious illness, of persistent coughing, of infants' coffins, of young men languishing in unemployment, of increase in juvenile delinquency (an inheritance from the urban world of the white man), of a demand for greater police services stemming, to a large degree, from a liquor problem that may itself be an adjunct of unemployment and other indicia of depression and demoralization.
That was a plain and blunt comment on the facts of life in the Northwest Territories. I have seen them. Forty years ago I made a trip into the northland on a river boat with a judicial party, and there was evidence then of a serious crisis as far as illness was concerned. Nevertheless, the native people stood tall and high. They were able to make a living by trapping and had a degree of independence which does not exist today. In the period of 40 years I have seen nothing to indicate that the civilization of the white man has done anything for them, nor is there any promise of it in this pitiful legislation.
In light of those facts, what was recommended in the Carrothers Commission report? It pointed out what was said by the Economic Council of Canada about the urgent need to make available additional financial resources to the government of the lower-income areas of the country, and it recommended that "there be a department of economic development and finance within the territorial government". Government supporters may say this recommendation has been met in part by this bill and previous bills. I say, "nonsense, it is not so." The report continues, at page 176:

And so on. One of the major factors would be the establishment of a Northwest Territories Development Corporation. I do not want to call up shades of the languishing Canada Development Corporation, but there is no doubt that capital is desperately required to provide a substantial foundation for the devel-opmen.t of the type of industry and economic activities which would persuade our young people to go north and make a contribution there. In the Soviet Union there has been a great deal of this activity. The carrot, so to speak, which the Soviet Union uses to entice young people to northern Siberia is certain types of opportunities not available in other parts of the Soviet Union. But that does not occur in the Northwest Territories. Apparently those who administer the affairs of the territories could not care less about this.

What a wonderful opportunity there would be if our young people who today are frustrated, worried and undecided about the kind of world we are making for them, could go to the north and make that contribution which is so essential and which needs to be made by young people who have something to offer. But the bill does not mention that at all. Nothing has been said about this in the speeches which have been made. I give the minister credit for being interested in the north. Although I have not made as many trips to the north recently as I should have liked, I think he will agree when I say that there is tremendous opportunity for our young people to go in and make a contribution so that the northern part of Canada will become what it should be, a great resource development area where liaison between north and south will contribute to the welfare of this country.
This will require money, because it cannot be done without funds. I know that not many people live there, but we must get them there. We talk much about pollution. Today the hon. member for Skeena talked about pollution. As our population concentrates more and more in the large metropolitan areas, the dangers of pollution become greater. When large numbers of people are concentrated in small land areas, the dangers of pollution are greatest. There are great advantages to decentralizing our population in the

Mr. Speaker, keeping an eye on the clock I should like to say a few words this evening and, hopefully, later about this most important piece of legislation affecting northern Canada.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
We welcome this bill, Mr. Speaker. We welcome the fact that the government has moved according to schedule in bringing these most important amendments relating to the future of the councils of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories prior to the forthcoming elections which are to be held later this year in both territories. We see that the amendments will provide, in the case of the Northwest Territories, an increased council and a reduction in the number of appointed members. They will give a number of powers to the council which the council has not had up to this point.
I wish to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). I welcome his participation in the movement of more responsibility into northern Canada. We welcome his initiatives which started a year ago last April, as he said earlier, in bringing the administration of justice and all its related functions closer to the people in the north. The fact that justices of the peace will now be appointed by the commissioner in consultation with his officials, and no longer by recommendation, is most welcome. It was tedious and laborious to come all the way to Ottawa to have their appointments dealt with by the cabinet. In consequence, delays of many months were caused in the appointment of these junior judicial officials in the territories. I think these initiatives will be welcomed in the north.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) has introduced a number of amendments to the Territorial Lands Act. I believe that this initiative is long overdue. However, in view of the great surge of economic and resource development throughout northern Canada in this day and age, I believe that the kind of ideas the minister has to protect the sensitive environment of the north to ensure that the ecology of northern Canada is not affected by resource development is something that will

be welcomed by conservationists throughout Canada, Canadians generally and northern people particularly.
Too long in the past we have watched man's effect on the environment as he has searched for the riches of the earth. We have seen trails across the tundra, the damming of creeks and the change of the environment, ecology and geography. We have wondered when man would be intelligent or smart enough to take some strong action to ensure that these sensitive areas of our country are protected for eternity. The minister has not as yet indicated what the regulations will be. However, if we read the proposed amendments in this bill we will see that the regulations should do the kind of job that all of us expect. I hope there will be the kind of land management, if I may use that term, that will protect, quoting from the bill-
-the ecological balance or physical characteristics of any area, set apart and appropriate any territorial lands in that area as a land management) zone.
In fairness to the mineral resource companies which have wandered through the north for the past 100 years, I suggest that they have protected the environment to the best of their ability within the regulations set down by the government. I hope that when the minister is discussing some of these aspects before the committee he will take a look at the staking and other regulations which of necessity at the moment require a disturbance of the physical characteristics of the area where work is being done.
The proposed amendments affecting the councils of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories have gone reasonably far. However, as I have said before in this House and in other places, I am concerned about two particular aspects. I congratulate the minister on increasing the number of elected members on the Northwest Territories Council from two to three. In November the minister said there would be two, and in May he said there would be three. On third reading I hope the minister will agree with the amendment which will be proposed to increase to four the number of elected members.
I hope that in the process of our discussions in committee we will come to some agreement and find a way around this dilemma of the Ottawa establishment being concerned about giving too much responsibility to the councils, and the dilemma of the councils being too concerned about wanting to be more involved

in their own affairs. What has happened in the past, in terms of transferring responsibility from the federal government to the territorial government, has been good. This government has acted fast and with decision following the publication of the Carrothers report. However, Mr. Speaker, regardless of the action which has been taken there is still one central, key issue. Somehow or other a means must be determined to give the elected members of both territories a viable say in the administration of their own affairs. The minister has indicated on a number of occasions that it is within his jurisdiction to establish executive councils and standing committees.
I will not argue with the minister about this. However, I am concerned, as are members of the councils, that the minister is torn between the natural reluctance of the people within his own department who advise him and the impatience of the members of both territorial councils. To my mind this is the central issue. We must and will face this issue in committee, that is, how to involve the elected members of the two councils in those things, as the minister said, which affect the quality of life-education, social development, local government, engineering and all those other functions which are properly and rightly the responsibility of the commissioner and the councils.
Having been an observer of the scene for a number of years, I believe that the commissioner and the public servants in the territorial government are to be congratulated on the manner in which they are accepting their responsibilities. They act with haste. They act with decision. And they are bringing, in my view, the real role of government to the people of the north who may not have had it when the federal administration was there.
